description: We are Team Aezakmi a collective and ambitious team looking to leave our mark by creating something that will have a lasting impact on the lives of people through the insightful usage of NASA data
summary:
Ignis-Atlassia answers the Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots challenge with a question scientists face every fire season: how do you compare two sensors without mistaking different resolutions, incomplete exports or processing gaps for changes in fire activity?
We built a web platform that imports NASA FIRMS standard records (MODIS Terra/Aqua and VIIRS Suomi NPP), keeps every original row with its version, UTC time, confidence and hash, and counts activity on a common 1 km grid in VIIRS-equivalent cell-days. A Sensor Bridge keeps MODIS-only, VIIRS-only, shared and gap days separate; FRP stays per sensor; unknown days are never shown as zero. Five workspaces (Explore, Investigate, Research Lab, Evidence and Research Studio) share one study over two million records from Northern California and Punjab–Haryana, 2006–2026, and every result exports as a frozen bundle a reviewer can recount. Research Studio is an agentic whiteboard: one command lets JARVIS, our tool-using AI copilot, arrange paired heat maps, charts, findings and original records into linked, evidence-bound cards, then draft a story and runnable workflow, without ever inventing a number.
It matters because red dots alone cannot answer “what is burning?” Comparable, traceable evidence can.
details:
What it does
Ignis-Atlassia answers the challenge question directly: how can MODIS and VIIRS hot spots be compared without mistaking different resolutions, incomplete exports or processing gaps for changes in fire activity? It imports NASA FIRMS standard-product records (MODIS Terra/Aqua Collection 6.1 and VIIRS Suomi NPP Collection 2), keeps every original row with its product version, UTC timestamp, confidence, FRP and file hash, and assigns each detection centroid to a common 1 km EPSG:6933 equal-area grid. The primary unit is VIIRS-equivalent active-fire cell-days per UTC day; MODIS-based estimates are labelled separately from observed VIIRS values, FRP is reported per sensor in MW/day and never added across sensors, and documented processing gaps (such as the July 24–29 2024 S-NPP notice) are treated as unknown, not zero. Our local archive holds about two million records (456,202 MODIS and 1,539,557 S-NPP) across two contrasting regions, Northern California and Punjab–Haryana, from 2006 to 2026.

How it works
Five connected workspaces share one applied study. Explore is the harmonised regional calendar with a Sensor Bridge that keeps MODIS-only, VIIRS-only, shared and gap days separate and compares a month against the median of comparable prior years. Investigate shows synchronised MODIS and VIIRS panes on a study-fixed heat scale, a UTC timeline, original rows and an optional 3D view. Research Lab covers daily overlap, candidate fire groups, grouping sensitivity and observation exposure. Evidence holds sources, method audit, calibration (count-ratio fits on 41 version-matched month pairs per region, with nested held-out results), native fire-mask validity for Park and Grove, and hash-bound MCD64A1 corroboration. Every displayed result can be downloaded as a frozen bundle and recounted by an offline verifier; changed inputs are rejected.

The agentic whiteboard
Research Studio is where the project becomes an agentic whiteboard. Its AI copilot, JARVIS, is a tool-using agent (Pydantic AI) with a registered catalogue of fifteen scientific operations: archive search, replay, harmonised calendar, missingness, compare, sensitivity, exposure, validation and more. The model never supplies a number: it cites a result ID and JSON pointer, and the backend resolves the actual value, unit and receipt. From Investigate, one Send to Canvas command captures the current view and JARVIS arranges paired sensor heat maps, daily charts, an availability timeline, checked findings and original records into eleven linked cards in four groups, then drafts a six-chapter story and a runnable seven-node workflow. Every card stays bound to a hash-bound evidence receipt; edits are revisioned transactions with object-level undo. JARVIS can explain a card, diagram a comparison, label a heatmap, find sources, point out what is missing or challenge a selected conclusion. The board exports to native .fireatlas.zip, editable Excalidraw, SVG, PNG and PDF; Story Director renders a captioned 1080p film; and a portable reader ships with a verifier that recomputes its figures from bundled receipts.

Benefits and intended impact
Scientists get reproducible cross-sensor comparison with provenance down to the row. Students and reviewers get a calendar and Sensor Bridge that make sensor differences visible instead of hiding them in a combined score. Presenters and communities get a traceable story rather than screenshots. The intended impact is a shared, evidence-bound place to work on NASA fire data, where “unknown” is a result, not a blank. Ignis-Atlassia is a research and learning tool, not an operational fire-management tool, and we say so in the interface.

Tools and technologies
Python (pyproj, pyshp, SQLite, NumPy for masks) for ingestion, counting, calibration and the HTTP service; an isolated Python 3.12 assistant runtime with Pydantic AI, FastMCP/MCP, Starlette and Uvicorn, with OpenAI, Google, free-only OpenRouter and AI& adapters under a daily cost ceiling. Frontend in HTML/CSS/JavaScript with Leaflet, plus an ArcGIS JS 4.32 terrain globe. Studio is a React 19 + TypeScript + Vite island using Excalidraw, tldraw, React Flow and Liveblocks; video uses Chromium, ffmpeg and Remotion; optional offline narration uses Piper. Verified by 305 Python tests, 48 frontend tests, seven renderer checks and Playwright browser audits, with GitHub Actions and Pages for the static demo. No special hardware; it runs in a browser.

What makes it creative
Most fire dashboards stop at dots on a map. We treat each detection as evidence with provenance, make disagreement between sensors a first-class view, and give the AI a seat on the whiteboard as a collaborator that can draw, arrange and argue, while being structurally unable to invent a number.

Factors we considered
Scientific honesty (hot spots are detected heat, not perimeters or proof of no fire; under-calibrated intervals are withheld rather than shown); reproducibility (frozen bundles, recount verifiers, checksums); comparability (one grid, one UTC day, study-fixed scales); privacy and safety (private boards, server-side credentials, bounded AI budgets); accessibility (keyboard navigation, narrow layouts, measured contrast); and licensing (Apache-2.0 code, NASA data credited separately). AI assistance (OpenAI Codex/ChatGPT) helped draft code and text; it did not create or alter any NASA values, and that is disclosed in the repository.
